name: Gödel Rotating Universe
description: An exact solution of Einstein's field equations describing a rotating dust universe with closed timelike curves.
convention: We work in units with $G = c = 1$ throughout. The parameter $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the dust, and $1/\omega$ is the one length of the solution. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $\lambda$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Kurt Gödel presented his rotating universe in the July 1949 issue of Reviews of Modern Physics, the issue dedicated to Einstein's seventieth birthday: a gift, as it were, that unsettled the honoree [godel1949]. The solution describes a universe filled with pressureless dust in uniform rotation, homogeneous in space and time, with no expansion. Its cosmological constant is negative, tuned to the density of the dust. About any world line of the dust the light cones tip as one moves outward, until at a critical radius they become tangent to a closed null curve, and beyond that radius closed timelike curves exist through every event: trajectories that loop back to their own past. Rotating dust had been solved before, by Kornel Lanczos in 1924 and by Willem Jacob van Stockum in 1937 [lanczos1924, vanstockum1937], but Gödel cites neither, and his universe is homogeneous where theirs is a cylinder turning about one axis.¶Gödel stated plainly in the paper that it is theoretically possible in these worlds to travel into the past [godel1949]. Gödel said more in the essay he wrote for the same birthday, in the volume Paul Arthur Schilpp gathered in Einstein's honor [godel1949idealistic]. By a round trip on a rocket ship in a sufficiently wide curve, he wrote, one could reach any region of the past, present, and future, though the velocities and the fuel such a trip would need were far beyond anything that could be expected ever to become a practical possibility. The trip was not his point.¶Relativity already seemed to him to prove the view of Parmenides, Kant, and the modern idealists that change is an illusion or an appearance due to our mode of perception. James Jeans had concluded from the cosmic time of the known cosmological solutions that there was no reason to abandon an absolute time lapsing objectively, and Gödel's answer was his own solutions, since the mere compatibility with the laws of nature of worlds with no distinguished absolute time throws light on the meaning of time in worlds where one can be defined. Einstein answered in the same volume that the essay was an important contribution to the analysis of the concept of time, that the problem had disturbed him already while he was building the general theory, and that it would be interesting to weigh whether such solutions are to be excluded on physical grounds [einstein1949remarks]. At the International Congress of Mathematicians in 1950 Gödel went on to rotating universes that also expand, as ours does, and showed that for them the absence of closed timelike lines is equivalent to the existence of a world time [godel1952].¶The first physicists to test the claim looked in the wrong place. Wolfgang Kundt worked out the geodesics of the solution in 1956 [kundt1956], and in 1961 Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and James Wright showed that none of the timelike ones closes, which they took to tell against Gödel's conclusion [chandrasekhar1961]. Howard Stein pointed out in 1970 that Gödel had never claimed a closed geodesic, since his travelers ride rockets, and that the objection rested on a misunderstanding [stein1970]. By then the solution was part of the canon. Stephen Hawking and George Ellis gave it a section of their treatise on the large scale structure of spacetime [hawking1973], and it holds its place in the standard catalogue of exact solutions [stephani2003]. Marcelo Rebouças and Jayme Tiomno showed in 1983 which metrics of Gödel's form share its homogeneity in space and time [reboucas1983], and in 2003 István Ozsváth and Engelbert Schucking redrew its light cones, correcting a picture in the standard literature [ozsvath2003].¶David Malament took up again the acceleration and fuel needed for the trip, and in 1984 set out what time travel in the Gödel universe does and does not involve [malament1984]. In 1985 he proved that every closed timelike curve in it demands a minimum total acceleration, so that a rocket flying one must spend at least three quarters of its initial mass as fuel [malament1985]. John Byron Manchak showed in 2011 that a curve allowed a single kink can do with less acceleration than Malament had conjectured any closed timelike curve must have [manchak2011].¶Neal Stephenson names it outright in Anathem: when the avout of Arbre and the Laterran Jules Verne Durand work out between them that a spaceship in a universe that happens to be rotating, if it travels far and fast enough, will travel backwards in time, a result the avout know and had always thought little more than a curiosity, Durand tells them that on his world it was discovered by "a kind of Saunt named Gödel: a friend of the Saunt who had earlier discovered geometrodynamics" [stephenson2008]. The Gödel universe is not a serious model of the cosmos we inhabit, since it does not expand and we observe expansion, but it remains one of the most important exact solutions in the theory. It showed that Einstein's field equations permit closed timelike curves through every event of a universe filled with rotating dust.

related.text: Rotating dust with closed timelike curves, found before Gödel's. It is a cylinder turning about one axis, and Gödel's universe is homogeneous [lanczos1924, vanstockum1937].
Every event of Gödel's universe is a Malament-Hogarth event, one with a worldline of infinite proper length in its past [earman1993].

The other universe of dust that neither expands nor contracts. Gödel wrote that the two are the only spatially homogeneous solutions with matter whose world lines stay equidistant, and that his cosmological constant has the opposite sign to Einstein's [godel1949].

Gödel's universe is a line times a space of three dimensions, and Gödel described that space as one of constant curvature, which is anti-de Sitter space, stretched by $\sqrt{2}$ along a family of timelike lines [godel1949]. Marianne Rooman and Philippe Spindel showed in 1998 that anti-de Sitter space is the boundary between the stretchings that are causally safe and those with closed timelike curves [rooman1998].
A time machine made to start at a definite moment, inside a finite region of vacuum. Amos Ori set it against Gödel's universe, which holds its closed timelike curves from the start [ori2005].

Charged dust in rigid rotation, homogeneous as Gödel's universe is, with a line element one term away from flat space. It is the member $m = 0$ of the family in which Gödel's is $m^2 = 2\Omega^2$ [som1968, reboucas1983].

A cloud of rigidly rotating dust with no cosmological constant, flat far away and singular at its centre. Its closed timelike curves stay inside a torus about that centre, where Gödel's pass through every event [bonnor1977cloud, astesiano2024].

coordinates.name: Cartesian
coordinates.convention: The coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$ are dimensionless, as the argument of $e^x$ forces.

coordinates.name: Cylindrical
domains: \sinh r = 1 \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, z \text{ are null)}
coordinates.convention: We use Kurt Gödel's own coordinates $(t, r, \phi, z)$, cylindrical about one world line of the dust, with $t$, $r$, and $z$ dimensionless and $\phi$ an angle.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = \dfrac{2}{\omega^2}\left(-dt^2 + dr^2 + \left(\sinh^2 r - \sinh^4 r\right)d\phi^2 - 2\sqrt{2}\sinh^2 r\,dt\,d\phi + dz^2\right)
